headline: White House still exploring hemp rules as 11 December deadline nears
dek: A White House spokeswoman said on 17 November the administration is still exploring federal hemp rules, but gave no plan or date before the 11 December limits.
key_points: White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the administration continues to explore a science-based federal framework for hemp for veterans and patients.
She gave no timeline, no draft and no answer on whether all marijuana will be moved to Schedule III, according to The Marijuana Herald.
The second phase of the federal hemp restriction takes effect on 11 December unless Congress acts, 23 days after the statement.
Without a bill text from the White House, the industry's hopes rest on lawmakers adding hemp language to the next funding bill.
body: The White House has repeated that President Trump supports cannabis and hemp reform, but it has not said what it will do before the federal hemp restriction takes full effect on 11 December. In comments to the cannabis outlet GreenState published on 17 November, and relayed by The Marijuana Herald, spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the administration continues to explore a hemp framework built on what it calls a Gold Science Standard, to widen treatment options for veterans and patients.

Asked whether the president still expects marijuana as a whole to be moved to Schedule III, Schuster pointed back to past actions rather than to new ones: the executive order Trump signed in December 2025 and a Truth Social post from April 2026. The Herald reports she gave no definite answer and no timeline.
## What the White House said, and what it did not

The statement is short on detail. There is no draft framework, no named agency lead and no indication of whether the administration wants a delay, a regulatory system or a mix of both. What it does confirm is that hemp is still on the White House's list, three weeks before most intoxicating hemp products face federal limits.

The December 2025 executive order is the clearest guide to the administration's thinking. According to the Herald's summary, it told federal officials to work with Congress on revising hemp rules and named options such as limits on THC per serving, caps per container and required ratios of CBD to THC. In June 2026 the White House wrote to House Speaker Mike Johnson asking Congress to revise the hemp rules, and it backed the delay that moved the restriction's main deadline to 11 December. In August, a senior Trump adviser said he supported federal rules for hemp-derived THC drinks, with similar protections for edibles and tinctures.
> The White House keeps saying hemp should be regulated, not banned, but it has not sent Congress the words to do it.

The federal restriction comes from the 2025 law that redefined hemp around total THC. Its first phase took effect on 12 November, as we reported that day, removing products made with cannabinoids that cannot be produced naturally by the plant, such as THC-O. The second phase, due on 11 December, is the one that reaches most hemp THC drinks, edibles and many full-spectrum CBD products. By our count, that is 23 days after Schuster's statement.

The deadline is tied to the federal budget. A stopgap funding law signed on 2 September moved the date from 12 November to 11 December, according to The Marijuana Herald, and that stopgap expires on the same day. As we reported on 16 November, Rep. James Comer of Kentucky has said the next funding bill is hemp's best chance of a fix. Several stand-alone bills are pending, including H.R. 7024, H.R. 7010, S. 3686 and H.R. 6209, but none has moved to a floor vote.

Support for regulation over a ban has been building. As we reported on 17 November, 26 veterans organisations and veteran-owned businesses, including the VFW, asked Congress to regulate hemp THC with testing, labelling and age limits instead of letting the restriction take effect. That framing matches the White House's own language about veterans and patients, which may give lawmakers political cover to add hemp language to a must-pass bill.

States are not waiting. As we reported, Missouri's own hemp THC law took effect on 12 November, and Iowa said on 16 November it will drop products above the federal cap from its state list. Each state move narrows the market regardless of what Congress does.

Schuster's comments also touched on marijuana rescheduling, which runs on a different track. State-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved cannabis products are already in Schedule III. The broader question of moving all marijuana there is in the hands of the Drug Enforcement Administration: Chief Administrative Law Judge Derek Julius is expected to issue a recommendation, and DEA Administrator Terrance Cole will decide. The White House statement offered nothing new on timing.

For hemp brands and the retailers that stock them, the statement changes little on the ground. Inventory and production plans for December still have to assume the restriction takes effect on schedule. A White House endorsement of specific language, such as per-serving THC limits, would be the signal that a deal is close, because it would give Republican leaders in Congress something concrete to attach to the funding bill.

Watch the text of the next stopgap or full-year funding bill, which must pass by 11 December, for any hemp section. Watch for a White House draft or a named official leading the hemp framework. And watch the DEA hearing docket for Judge Julius's recommendation on broader rescheduling.
